title: The Pantheon in Rome now needs a ticket: how entry works, and who still gets in free
subtitle: For centuries you walked straight in. Since July 2023 there is a ticket, a line and a few exceptions worth knowing.
excerpt: The Pantheon in Rome has charged for entry since July 2023. How the ticket works, who still enters free, what a fast track ticket really spares you, and what to look at once you are under the dome.
longtail_phrases: do you need a ticket for the Pantheon in Rome
is the Pantheon in Rome still free
how long does a visit to the Pantheon take
can you visit the Pantheon during Mass
does it rain inside the Pantheon
meta_title: The Pantheon in Rome needs a ticket: how entry works
meta_description: The Pantheon has charged for entry since July 2023. How the ticket works, who gets in free, what fast track means, and what to see inside.

featured_image.alt: The porch and the drum of the Pantheon in Rome seen across Piazza della Rotonda, with the fountain and its obelisk on the left

content_html:
[place attraction="pantheon-rome" city="rome"]

The bronze letters across the front of the Pantheon say that Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, built it when he was consul for the third time. That is true of a temple that once stood here, and not of this one. Agrippa's building burned, and so did its replacement. What you see was put up under the emperor Hadrian, between about AD 118 and 125, and Hadrian, who rarely signed anything he built, had the old name set back on the front.

It has been in use ever since, which is why it is still standing. In 609 the emperor Phocas gave the temple to Pope Boniface IV, who made it a church, St Mary and the Martyrs. For the next fourteen centuries anyone could walk in from the square. That ended on 3 July 2023, when a ticket was introduced. The building has not changed. The way in has.

What changed in 2023

The Pantheon belongs to the Italian state and is also a working church. Since July 2023 sightseers pay for entry, under an agreement between the Ministry of Culture and the diocese of Rome. The ticket is a plain entry ticket: no guide and no audio come with it.

It is sold in two ways: online, on the ministry's own museum ticket site, and at the door. The door is where the line forms, and in the warm months it can run round the fountain. People who already hold a ticket are checked in separately.

Who still gets in free

  • Children and teenagers under eighteen. They still need to be counted at the entrance, so take them through the ticket point with you.
  • Residents of the city of Rome.
  • People attending Mass. The Pantheon holds services at the weekend and on feast days. Worshippers are let in for the service, and sightseeing stops while it lasts.
  • Everybody, on the first Sunday of the month, when state museums and monuments in Italy are free. The line that day is the longest of the month.

Young adults from the European Union have had a reduced rate. Bring an identity document if you claim any of these.

What "fast track" means here

There is no secret door. The building has one entrance, between the columns of the porch, and everyone passes it. A ticket bought beforehand spares you the ticket line, which is the slow one. It does not spare you the check at the door, and on a crowded afternoon that still takes some minutes.

Two things can close the doors without notice to sightseers: a service, and an official ceremony at the royal tombs. If your day is tight, go early. The first hour after opening is the quietest, and the last hour before closing is the next best.

The porch: each column shaft is a single piece of Egyptian granite. Photo: Nicholas Hartmann, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What to look at inside

A visit takes twenty to thirty minutes. It is one room, and it rewards standing still.

The dome

The inside is as high as it is wide: about 43 metres from the floor to the opening, and the same across. A sphere of that size would fit inside exactly. The dome is concrete with no steel in it, and nobody has built a larger one that way since. The builders made it lighter as it rose, mixing heavy stone into the base and pumice into the top, and the square coffers take out more weight.

The dome from the floor: five rings of coffers and the open oculus. Photo: T. Le Berre, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The oculus

The opening at the top, about nine metres wide, is the only window. It has never had glass. A disc of sunlight crosses the walls and the floor through the day, and when it rains, it rains inside. The floor is slightly domed, and small holes in the marble carry the water away.

The marble floor under the oculus, with the small holes that carry off the rain. Photo: Wknight94, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The tombs

Raphael asked to be buried here and was, in 1520, at the age of thirty-seven. His tomb is on the left as you face the altar, under a statue of the Virgin he ordered for it. Two kings of united Italy, Victor Emmanuel II and Umberto I, lie in the large niches, with Queen Margherita.

The tomb of Raphael, who died in Rome in 1520. Photo: Ank Kumar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The porch, on the way out

Sixteen columns hold up the porch, and each shaft is a single piece of granite quarried in Egypt and shipped across the Mediterranean. The roof of the porch once had bronze beams. Pope Urban VIII, of the Barberini family, had them melted down in the 1620s, mostly for cannon. Rome answered with a line still quoted: what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.

Church rules

This is a consecrated church, and the staff may ask you to cover bare shoulders and to keep your voice down. Hats off for men. Photographs are allowed. There are a few benches, and no cloakroom to speak of, so do not arrive with luggage.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A fast track ticket is entry, booked ahead. The listing gives little detail, so read on the booking page how and where the ticket is delivered.
  • An entry ticket with an audio tour and a city walk names the ticket in its title, while the list of what is included speaks only of the audio tour. Read that list before you pay, and choose the plain ticket if it is not clear.
  • A combined ticket with Castel Sant'Angelo covers the papal fortress on the Tiber as well, twenty minutes away on foot.
  • The Pantheon audio tour is an hour of commentary on your own phone, in eleven stops. It does not include entry.
  • The audio walk that ends at the Pantheon is a route through ancient Rome from the Circus Maximus. No tickets are part of it.

Opening hours and the days with services are on our page for the Pantheon.

From here

Behind the building, in Piazza della Minerva, a small marble elephant designed by Bernini carries an obelisk on its back, in front of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. Two minutes to the west, the church of San Luigi dei Francesi has three paintings by Caravaggio in one chapel, and entry is free. Piazza Navona is five minutes on, and the Trevi Fountain ten minutes the other way. For the rest of Rome, open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Nicholas Hartmann, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Do you need a ticket for the Pantheon in Rome?
faqs.a: Yes. Since 3 July 2023 sightseers need an entry ticket, sold online and at the door. Before that date entry was free for everyone.

faqs.q: Is the Pantheon in Rome still free for anyone?
faqs.a: It is free for visitors under eighteen, for residents of Rome, for people attending Mass, and for everybody on the first Sunday of the month. Bring an identity document.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to the Pantheon take?
faqs.a: Twenty to thirty minutes inside. Add the time in line, which is short early in the morning and can be long at midday in season.

faqs.q: Can you visit the Pantheon during Mass?
faqs.a: Not as a sightseer. The Pantheon is a church, and visits stop while a service is held. People who come to attend the Mass are admitted for it.

faqs.q: Does it rain inside the Pantheon?
faqs.a: Yes. The opening at the top of the dome has no glass, so rain falls on the floor, which is slightly domed and has small drain holes in the marble.

title: Pitti Palace and Boboli Gardens: which ticket you need, and how to split half a day
subtitle: The palace and the gardens behind it are two visits with two tickets. What each one opens, and in which order to do them.
excerpt: The Pitti Palace and the Boboli Gardens in Florence are sold separately. What the palace ticket opens, what the garden ticket opens, when a combined ticket makes sense, and how to fit both into half a day.
focus_keyword: Pitti Palace and Boboli Gardens ticket
longtail_phrases: does the Pitti Palace ticket include the Boboli Gardens
how long do you need for the Pitti Palace and Boboli Gardens
is the Boboli Gardens worth it
what to see in the Palatine Gallery
which day is the Pitti Palace closed
meta_title: Pitti Palace and Boboli Gardens: which ticket you need
meta_description: The Pitti Palace and the Boboli Gardens have separate tickets. What each one opens, when to combine them, and how to do both in half a day.

featured_image.alt: The long rusticated stone front of the Pitti Palace in Florence across its sloping square

content_html:
[place attraction="palazzo-pitti" city="florence"]

Luca Pitti was a banker, and for a time the most powerful ally the Medici had. About 1458 he began a palace on the far side of the Arno, on rising ground, meant to be larger than anything his friends owned. The story Florentines told later was that he wanted windows as big as the Medici's front door. He lost his standing, ran short of money, and died in 1472 with the building unfinished.

In 1549 his heirs sold it. The buyer was Eleonora of Toledo, wife of Duke Cosimo I de' Medici, who wanted air and a garden for a large family. So the palace built to outdo the Medici became their home, and then the home of every ruler of Tuscany after them. They enlarged it for three centuries and filled it with pictures, and behind it they laid out a garden up the hill. Today these are two separate visits, sold with two separate tickets, and that is where most confusion begins.

Two tickets, not one

There is one ticket office, on the right-hand side of the front on Piazza Pitti, and it sells different things:

  • The palace ticket opens the museums inside the building: the Palatine Gallery, which is the reason to come, the Gallery of Modern Art on the top floor, the Treasury of the Grand Dukes on the ground floor, and the Museum of Costume and Fashion. It does not open the gardens.
  • The Boboli ticket opens the gardens behind the palace, the small Porcelain Museum at the top of them, and the Bardini Garden, a second hillside garden ten minutes' walk to the east. It does not open the palace.
  • A combined ticket covers both, and there is a wider one that adds the Uffizi and runs over several days in a row. Check how many days, and whether each place can be entered once only.

The palace is closed on Mondays. The gardens keep a calendar of their own, with closing days that do not match the palace, and they shut earlier in winter. On the first Sunday of the month both are free and both are crowded.

The palace: where to spend your time

Go to the Palatine Gallery first, on the main floor. It is unlike the Uffizi. The pictures are not arranged by date or school. They hang as the grand dukes hung them, frame against frame up to the cornice, in rooms with painted ceilings and silk on the walls.

  • The planet rooms. Five rooms in a row, named after Venus, Apollo, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, with ceilings painted by Pietro da Cortona in the 1640s. The best pictures are here.
  • Raphael. The round Madonna of the Chair, in the Saturn room, and the portrait known as the Veiled Woman.
  • Titian. The portrait of a young man with grey eyes, called the Young Englishman, and the woman in a blue dress known as La Bella.
  • Rubens. The Consequences of War, painted in 1638, in which Mars pulls away from Venus while Europe throws up her arms.
  • Caravaggio. A small, dark Sleeping Cupid, painted in Malta.
  • Canova. The marble Venus in the middle of the Venus room.

Allow an hour and a half. The other museums in the building are worth the stairs only if you have a particular interest in them.

One of the state rooms of the palace: stucco, columns and chandeliers. Photo: Dimitris Kamaras, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The gardens: a walk uphill

The Boboli Gardens were begun in 1549 for Eleonora and became the model for the court gardens of Europe. They are large and steep. The paths are gravel, there is little shade on the main axis, and you gain a good deal of height. Wear proper shoes and carry water.

  • The amphitheatre. Directly behind the palace, in the hollow left by the quarry that supplied its stone. An Egyptian obelisk stands in the middle, brought from the Villa Medici in Rome in 1790.
  • The climb. Straight up past the Fountain of Neptune to the statue of Abundance. Turn round here: the palace is below you, and the cathedral dome beyond it.
  • The Knight's Garden. At the very top, a small walled garden with the Porcelain Museum and a view over olive groves to the south.
  • The cypress avenue and the Isolotto. A long straight avenue runs down the western slope to an oval pool with an island in it.
  • The Great Grotto. Near the exit, built by Bernardo Buontalenti between 1583 and 1593. Michelangelo's unfinished Prisoners stood in its corners until 1909, when they went to the Accademia. The figures there now are copies.

The full loop takes an hour and a half to two hours.

The amphitheatre behind the palace, cut into the hollow of an old quarry. Photo: Rufus46, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The reward for the climb: the cathedral dome over the roofs of the city. Photo: Txllxt TxllxT, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Isolotto, the pool at the far end of the gardens. Photo: Armin Kleiner, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Half a day, in the right order

In the warm months, do the gardens first, as soon as they open, and go into the palace when the sun is high. In winter, reverse it: the gardens close early, so see them before the light goes, but not at the very end of the day. Either way, allow three and a half to four hours for both, and take a break between them. If you have two hours only, choose one. On a hot or wet day choose the Palatine Gallery. On a clear spring morning choose the gardens.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A Pitti Palace ticket with a Palatine Gallery audio tour is the palace ticket, with all the museums in the building, and commentary for the main gallery on your own phone. The gardens are not part of it.
  • A ticket for the Pitti Palace, the Boboli and the Bardini Gardens with a sightseeing audio tour opens all three. Read the exclusions: the audio is a walk through the city and does not cover the inside of the palace.
  • A highlights tour with a Boboli Gardens ticket is the garden ticket with a city audio walk. The voucher is swapped for a ticket at the palace ticket office. The palace is not included.
  • A combined skip the line ticket with the Uffizi covers the Uffizi, the palace and the gardens. The listing says little, so check the days of validity before you book.
  • The Palatine Gallery highlights audio tour is commentary only, with no entry.

These are the Pitti Palace and Boboli Gardens tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="palazzo-pitti" match="pitti,boboli" limit="5"]

Hours change with the season: see our pages for the Pitti Palace and the Boboli Gardens.

From here

You are on the quieter bank of the river. The church of Santo Spirito, the last that Brunelleschi designed, is five minutes west, on a square with a morning market. The Ponte Vecchio is five minutes north, with the Vasari Corridor running over it from the palace towards the Uffizi. See what else there is in Florence, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Suicasmo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Does the Pitti Palace ticket include the Boboli Gardens?
faqs.a: No. The palace ticket opens the museums inside the building. The gardens have their own ticket, which also covers the Bardini Garden. A combined ticket covers both.

faqs.q: How long do you need for the Pitti Palace and the Boboli Gardens?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half for the Palatine Gallery and an hour and a half to two hours for the gardens. With a break, allow half a day for both.

faqs.q: What should you see in the Palatine Gallery?
faqs.a: The five planet rooms with ceilings by Pietro da Cortona, Raphael's Madonna of the Chair and Veiled Woman, Titian's portraits, Rubens's Consequences of War and Caravaggio's Sleeping Cupid.

faqs.q: Are the Boboli Gardens worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, in good weather and if you do not mind walking uphill. They are large and steep, with views over Florence from the top. In heat or rain the palace is the better choice.

faqs.q: Which day is the Pitti Palace closed?
faqs.a: The palace is closed on Mondays. The gardens have closing days of their own, so check both before you plan the visit.

title: The Picasso Museum in Barcelona: what you will see, what you will not, and which ticket to book
subtitle: It holds the boy and the young man, not the famous cubist. Knowing that before you go changes the visit.
excerpt: The Picasso Museum in Barcelona shows how Picasso became Picasso: his teenage paintings, the Blue Period and the Las Meninas series. What is there, what is elsewhere, how timed tickets and free hours work, and what each listing includes.
focus_keyword: Picasso Museum Barcelona what to see
secondary_keywords: is the Picasso Museum Barcelona worth it
longtail_phrases: is the Picasso Museum in Barcelona worth it
what is in the Picasso Museum Barcelona
is Guernica in the Picasso Museum in Barcelona
when is the Picasso Museum in Barcelona free
how long does the Picasso Museum Barcelona take
meta_title: Picasso Museum Barcelona: what you see, which ticket
meta_description: What the Picasso Museum in Barcelona holds and what it does not, how timed tickets and the free hours work, and what each ticket includes.

featured_image.alt: A stone courtyard of the Picasso Museum in Barcelona seen through an arch, with a Gothic window above a lit doorway

content_html:
[place attraction="museu-picasso" city="barcelona"]

When the museum opened on Carrer de Montcada in March 1963, the name of Picasso was not the one put forward. Spain was ruled by Franco, and Picasso, who had painted Guernica and sworn not to return while the dictator lived, was not a man the regime wished to honour. So the city presented the new museum as the collection of Jaume Sabartés, a Barcelona friend of his youth who had become his secretary, and who gave the hundreds of works he owned to start it.

Picasso never saw it. He was eighty-one, lived in France, and had last been in Barcelona in 1934. He sent pictures instead: when Sabartés died in 1968 he gave a whole series in his memory, and in 1970 he gave everything his family had kept in the city since he was a boy. That history explains what hangs here, and it is the first thing to know before you buy a ticket.

What you will see

The collection, more than four thousand works, is strongest at the beginning. It follows a child who could draw like an adult until the moment he stopped wanting to. The rooms run in order of time.

  • The teenager. Picasso came to Barcelona in 1895, at thirteen, when his father took a post at the city's art school. First Communion, painted at fourteen, and Science and Charity, a large hospital scene painted at fifteen, are exactly what a jury of the day wanted. He could have had that career.
  • The young man about town. Portraits of friends, small street and café scenes, and the first trips to Paris, from the years around his first exhibition in 1900.
  • The Blue Period. A handful of pictures from 1901 to 1904, the years in which he moved between Barcelona and Paris before leaving for good.
  • The return in 1917. He came back for some months with the Russian Ballet. The Harlequin from that stay was his gift to the city, and the first Picasso to enter a public collection in Spain.
  • Las Meninas. In 1957, in the south of France, he shut himself away with a single painting by Velázquez and produced fifty-eight canvases from it in a few months. The whole series is here, in its own rooms, and it is the one part of the museum that shows the Picasso everyone knows.
  • Prints and ceramics. Rooms of engravings, and pottery given by his widow Jacqueline.

A courtyard with its open staircase to the main floor, the pattern of every palace on the street. Photo: haitham alfalah, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What you will not see

Guernica is in Madrid, at the Reina Sofía. Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, named after a street of brothels a few minutes from here, Carrer d'Avinyó, is in New York. The great cubist pictures are in Paris and elsewhere. If you come expecting them, you will be puzzled by rooms of careful portraits and seascapes.

So is it worth it? Yes, if you are curious about how a painter is made, or if Las Meninas alone sounds like a reason. It is less rewarding as a first meeting with Picasso, and children who do not already know his later work tend to lose interest by the third room.

The building is half of it

The museum fills five medieval palaces in a row. Carrer de Montcada was the street of Barcelona's richest merchants from the thirteenth century to the fifteenth, when the city traded across the whole Mediterranean. Each house follows the same plan: a plain front, a gate wide enough for a cart, a courtyard, and an open stone staircase to the main floor. You pass through several of these courtyards during the visit, and you may look into the first ones without a ticket.

Carrer de Montcada, the medieval merchants' street where the museum stands. Photo: Andrei Dan Suciu, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

The street front of the Aguilar palace, the first of the five the museum took over. Photo: Pere López, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

How the tickets work

  • Entry is timed. You book a slot. In spring and summer, and at weekends, the slots of the day are often gone by late morning.
  • Collection, or collection and exhibition. The standard ticket covers the permanent collection. Temporary exhibitions are sold with it as a fuller ticket, or separately.
  • Free hours exist, and must be booked. The museum has long opened without charge late on Thursday afternoons and on the first Sunday of the month. You still need a ticket for a slot, released online a few days before, and they go quickly.
  • Monday is the closing day.

Allow an hour and a half. Large bags go into lockers. The streets around are narrow and busy, so keep your phone and wallet out of back pockets.

Reading the partner's listings

  • An entry ticket is entry to the museum and nothing else. The listing does not say whether temporary exhibitions are covered, so read the booking page.
  • A ticket with an audio tour and a walk through El Born includes entry, commentary for the museum in the partner's app, and an audio walk through the quarter outside.
  • A ticket with an audio tour and a city walk is close to the first: entry, a route through the rooms, and a walk. The commentary covers the permanent collection, not the temporary exhibition.
  • The listings called only "audio tour", of the museum, or of the museum and El Born, do not include entry. You book your slot yourself.

[partner attraction="museu-picasso" match="picasso" limit="5"]

Current hours are on our page for the Picasso Museum.

From here

At the bottom of the street stands Santa Maria del Mar, built between 1329 and 1383 by the people of the quarter, the purest Gothic church in the city. A few minutes east, the old Born market shelters the excavated streets of the district pulled down after the siege of 1714, and the ground floor is free to walk through. Els Quatre Gats, the café where Picasso held his first exhibition, is ten minutes away, near the cathedral. For the rest of Barcelona, open the trip planner for Spain.

Santa Maria del Mar, three minutes from the museum. Photo: Kent Wang, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Cover photo: Enric, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Picasso Museum in Barcelona worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want to see how Picasso developed: his teenage paintings, the Blue Period and the complete Las Meninas series. It holds few of his famous cubist works, so it is less suited as a first introduction.

faqs.q: Is Guernica in the Picasso Museum in Barcelona?
faqs.a: No. Guernica is in Madrid, at the Reina Sofía museum. The Barcelona museum's largest late work is the Las Meninas series of 1957.

faqs.q: When is the Picasso Museum in Barcelona free?
faqs.a: It has long been free late on Thursday afternoons and on the first Sunday of the month. Free tickets for a time slot must still be reserved online and run out fast.

faqs.q: How long does the Picasso Museum in Barcelona take?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half for the permanent collection. Add half an hour if you also visit a temporary exhibition.

faqs.q: Do you need to book the Picasso Museum in advance?
faqs.a: It is wise. Entry is by time slot, and in spring, summer and at weekends the slots for the same day are often sold out by late morning.

title: Reina Sofía or Thyssen: which museum to add to the Prado, and how to see Guernica
subtitle: Three museums stand within ten minutes of each other in Madrid. Most visitors have time for two.
excerpt: After the Prado, Madrid offers two more great museums a short walk away. What the Reina Sofía and the Thyssen-Bornemisza each hold, how to find Guernica, which one suits which visitor, and what the tickets include.
secondary_keywords: where to see Guernica in Madrid
Madrid art museums which to visit
longtail_phrases: is the Reina Sofía or the Thyssen better
where is Guernica in the Reina Sofía
can you do the Prado and the Thyssen in one day
how long does the Reina Sofía take
which day is the Reina Sofía closed
meta_title: Reina Sofía or Thyssen: which to add to the Prado
meta_description: What the Reina Sofía and the Thyssen each hold, how to find Guernica, which museum suits you after the Prado, and what the tickets include.

featured_image.alt: The stone front of the Reina Sofía museum in Madrid, a former hospital, with two glass lift towers attached to it

content_html:
[place attraction="museo-nacional-centro-de-arte-reina-sofia" city="madrid"]

On the afternoon of 26 April 1937, a market day, German and Italian aircraft fighting for General Franco bombed the Basque town of Gernika for some three hours. Pablo Picasso, in Paris, had been asked by the Spanish Republic for a mural for its pavilion at that summer's world fair, and had not yet settled on a subject. He began drawing within days and finished in about five weeks: a canvas nearly eight metres long, in black, white and grey.

After the fair the painting travelled, and spent four decades on loan in New York. Picasso had laid down that it should go to Spain only when the country was free again. It arrived in September 1981, six years after Franco's death, and has hung since 1992 in the Reina Sofía. That one picture decides the question for many visitors. For the rest, here is how the two museums differ.

Three museums, ten minutes apart

The Prado, the Thyssen-Bornemisza and the Reina Sofía stand along the same avenue. The Thyssen is across the square from the Prado, five minutes on foot. The Reina Sofía is ten minutes further south, facing Atocha station.

They divide the history of painting between them. The Prado holds the old masters of the Spanish crown, up to Goya. The Reina Sofía takes over where the Prado stops: the twentieth century, mostly Spanish. The Thyssen is one family's collection and covers seven centuries, including everything the other two lack.

The Reina Sofía: Guernica and the Spanish century

The main building was Madrid's General Hospital, an eighteenth-century block round a garden courtyard, to which glass lifts were added on the outside. A red extension by Jean Nouvel opened behind it in 2005.

Guernica is on the second floor. Go straight up. The room is long and always busy, and a guard keeps people back from the canvas. Do not stop at the painting alone: on the walls nearby are the sketches Picasso made on the way, and the photographs Dora Maar took of the canvas at each stage, which show him moving the bull and raising the arm with the lamp. The rules on taking pictures in this room have changed more than once, so read the signs.

On the same floor are Dalí, with the Girl at the Window of 1925 and The Great Masturbator of 1929, Miró, and the cubist still lifes of Juan Gris. Two hours cover the floor well. The floors above, with art after 1945, are for those with a taste for it.

The museum is closed on Tuesdays. It has long opened free in the last two hours of the day and on Sunday afternoon, and the line for those hours forms early.

The garden in the middle of the old hospital, a quiet place between two floors. Photo: Carmen Voces, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Thyssen: seven centuries in one house

Two barons Thyssen-Bornemisza, father and son, built up one of the great private collections of the last century at their villa in Lugano. Spain received it on loan in 1988, opened it in the Villahermosa Palace in 1992, and bought it the following year: nearly eight hundred paintings.

Start on the top floor and come down, and you walk from the thirteenth century to the 1960s. What makes it valuable in Madrid is what the Prado does not have:

  • Early Italian and Flemish pictures. Jan van Eyck's Annunciation, painted to look like two stone statues, and Ghirlandaio's profile portrait of Giovanna Tornabuoni.
  • The Renaissance north of the Alps. Holbein's portrait of Henry VIII, hardly larger than a book, and Carpaccio's Young Knight in a Landscape.
  • Caravaggio. His Saint Catherine of Alexandria.
  • Impressionists and after. Monet, Degas, Van Gogh's fields at Auvers from the last months of his life.
  • Americans. Nineteenth-century landscapes, and Edward Hopper's Hotel Room.
  • The twentieth century. German Expressionists, and Roy Lichtenstein's Woman in Bath.

Allow two to two and a half hours. The Thyssen is open every day, with a shorter Monday on which entry to the collection has long been free.

The Villahermosa Palace, on the Paseo del Prado, where the Thyssen opened in 1992. Photo: Luis García (Zaqarbal), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Ghirlandaio's portrait of Giovanna Tornabuoni, in the Thyssen. Photo: reproduction of a painting in the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Holbein's small portrait of Henry VIII, also in the Thyssen. Photo: reproduction of a painting in the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Which one, then

  • Choose the Reina Sofía if Guernica is on your list, if you care about Picasso, Dalí and Miró, or if you are travelling with teenagers who have had enough saints.
  • Choose the Thyssen if you like to see a little of everything, if Impressionism matters to you, or if the Prado left you wanting more old pictures from outside Spain.
  • On the same day as the Prado, the Thyssen is easier: it is next door and smaller. Do the Prado in the morning, eat, and cross the square.
  • With a second day, give the Reina Sofía its own morning, and go straight to the second floor while you are fresh.

The three museums also sell a joint pass for one visit to each. It pays only if you will enter all three.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A Reina Sofía entry ticket covers the collection and the temporary exhibitions, with no commentary.
  • A Reina Sofía ticket with an audio tour adds a route through the rooms in the partner's app, on your own phone. Bring earphones.
  • A Thyssen-Bornemisza ticket with an audio tour is the same pairing for the Thyssen.
  • The listings called only "audio tour", one for each museum, do not include entry. You buy that yourself.

Current hours are on our pages for the Reina Sofía and the Thyssen-Bornemisza.

From here

The Prado is between the two. Behind it, the Retiro park has a boating lake and the Crystal Palace, a glasshouse of 1887. Across the road from the Reina Sofía, the old hall of Atocha station holds a garden of tropical plants under its iron roof. For the rest of Madrid, open the trip planner for Spain.

Cover photo: Luis García (Zaqarbal), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 ES.

faqs.q: Is the Reina Sofía or the Thyssen better?
faqs.a: They do different things. The Reina Sofía is Spanish twentieth-century art, with Guernica. The Thyssen is a survey of seven centuries, strong where the Prado is not: early Flemish, Impressionist and American painting.

faqs.q: Where is Guernica in the Reina Sofía?
faqs.a: On the second floor of the main building, the old hospital. The sketches for it and the photographs of its stages hang in the rooms around.

faqs.q: Can you do the Prado and the Thyssen in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. They face each other across a square. Take the Prado in the morning and the Thyssen, which is smaller, after lunch.

faqs.q: How long does the Reina Sofía take?
faqs.a: About two hours for the second floor, with Guernica, Dalí and Miró. Add an hour if you go up to the art after 1945.

faqs.q: Which day is the Reina Sofía closed?
faqs.a: It is closed on Tuesdays. The Thyssen is open daily, with shorter hours on Mondays. Check the current hours before you go.

title: Montserrat from Barcelona by train: cable car or rack railway, and what needs a ticket at the top
subtitle: One train line, two stations, two ways up the mountain. You have to choose before you buy.

featured_image.alt: The monastery of Montserrat on its ledge under grey rock pinnacles, with the plain of Catalonia stretching out beyond

content_html:
[place attraction="santa-maria-de-montserrat-abbey" city="barcelona"]

The story goes that in the year 880, on several Saturday evenings, shepherd boys saw a light come down on the mountain and heard singing. A search of the place led to a cave, and in the cave to a statue of the Virgin. The bishop wanted it carried to the town of Manresa. Partway down, it became too heavy to move, which was taken as a clear enough instruction, and a chapel was built where it stopped.

The dates that can be checked begin in 1025, when Abbot Oliba founded a monastery on the ledge. The statue venerated today is a wooden figure of the twelfth century, darkened by age, and Catalans call her La Moreneta, the little dark one. Napoleon's troops wrecked the monastery in 1811 and 1812, and most of what stands was rebuilt afterwards. Monks still live here, some 700 metres up a mountain of pale rounded pinnacles, 50 kilometres from Barcelona. Getting there on your own is easy, once you understand one choice.

The train from Plaça d'Espanya

Take line R5 of the Catalan railways, the FGC, from the station under Plaça d'Espanya in Barcelona, in the direction of Manresa. Trains leave about once an hour and take about an hour. Leave by nine if you can: the mountain fills up from late morning.

The line has two stops for Montserrat, a few minutes apart, and each connects with a different way up:

  • Montserrat Aeri, the first, is the foot of the cable car.
  • Monistrol de Montserrat, the next, is where the rack railway starts.

Combined tickets, sold from the machines at Plaça d'Espanya and by resellers, are for one of the two. A cable car ticket is not accepted on the rack railway, and the other way round. Decide before you pay, and get off at the right station.

Cable car or rack railway

The cable car

The Aeri de Montserrat has been running since 1930. Its two yellow cabins climb the cliff in about five minutes, and the view is the best part of the journey. You stand, the cabins are small, and in season the wait at the bottom can be long. It stops in high wind, and closes for maintenance for a spell most winters.

The yellow cabin of the cable car, with the valley station far below. Photo: Bernard Gagnon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The rack railway

The Cremallera is a modern green train on a toothed rail, opened in 2003 on the route of a line that ran from 1892 to 1957. It takes about fifteen minutes, has seats and large windows, runs in any weather and takes pushchairs and wheelchairs without trouble.

The green trains of the rack railway, the other way up. Photo: NearEMPTiness, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

If the day is clear and you do not mind heights, take the cable car. With children, in bad weather, or if you dislike queues, take the rack railway. Both leave you a few steps from the monastery square.

What is free at the top, and what is not

The mountain, the square, the viewpoints and the walking paths cost nothing. The things most people come for have tickets:

  • The basilica. Sightseers now enter with a ticket for a time slot. Attending a service remains free.
  • The statue. A stair behind the altar leads up to the niche where La Moreneta sits, so that visitors can pass in front of her. That walk has had a ticket and a slot of its own, and its own line.
  • The boys' choir. The Escolania, a choir school recorded here since the fourteenth century, sings in the basilica around the middle of the day. Places are ticketed. The choir does not sing every day, and is away during school holidays, including a good part of the summer. Check before you build the day around it.
  • The museum. A surprising collection for a mountain: a Caravaggio, an El Greco, early Picasso, Monet.
  • The Sant Joan funicular. It climbs from the monastery to the ridge, where level paths lead to old hermitages and wide views.

Tickets for the basilica, the statue and the choir are limited, and on busy days they sell out. Book them for a time that leaves a margin after your train.

The Virgin of Montserrat in her niche above the altar, as you see her from the nave. Photo: José Luiz, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The funicular track climbing from the monastery towards the ridge. Photo: Yair Haklai, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A railway ticket with an abbey audio tour includes the return train from Barcelona and the rack railway, entry to the audiovisual exhibition, and an audio tour of the site on your own phone. The basilica, the statue and the choir are not listed.
  • An audio tour with a ticket to the choir includes the audiovisual exhibition and a place to hear the Escolania. Transport is not included.
  • A cable car return ticket with an audio tour covers the cable car up and down from Montserrat Aeri station. It does not include the train from Barcelona or any entry at the top.
  • An experience with a ticket to the throne of Our Lady lists a ticket to the basilica and the museums, with an audio tour. You make your own way there.
  • The abbey audio tour is commentary only.

How long, and what to bring

Count six to eight hours from Barcelona and back: an hour and a half each way, and three to four hours on the mountain. It is cooler and windier than the coast, so bring a layer even in summer, and shoes fit for a path. There are cafeterias, and stalls where farmers sell fresh cheese and honey. Note the time of the last train down before you set off on a walk.

Hours are on our pages for the abbey of Montserrat, the cable car and the museum.

From here

From the top station of the Sant Joan funicular, a marked path leads in a little over an hour to Sant Jeroni, the summit of the range at 1,236 metres. A gentler path from the monastery goes down to the Holy Cave of the legend, about forty minutes each way. Back in Barcelona, the train returns you to Plaça d'Espanya, at the foot of Montjuïc. To see what else is within a day's reach, open the attractions map of Spain.

faqs.q: How do you get to Montserrat from Barcelona by train?
faqs.a: Take FGC line R5 from Plaça d'Espanya towards Manresa, about an hour. Get off at Montserrat Aeri for the cable car or at Monistrol de Montserrat for the rack railway.

faqs.q: Is the cable car or the rack railway better for Montserrat?
faqs.a: The cable car is faster, about five minutes, with the better view, but you stand and may queue. The rack railway takes about fifteen minutes, has seats, and runs in any weather.

faqs.q: Do you need a ticket for the monastery of Montserrat?
faqs.a: The mountain, the square and the paths are free. Sightseers need a timed ticket for the basilica, and there are separate tickets for passing in front of the statue of the Virgin and for hearing the choir.

faqs.q: When does the Montserrat boys choir sing?
faqs.a: Around the middle of the day, on most days during the school year. The choir is away in school holidays, including much of the summer, so check the calendar before you travel.

faqs.q: How long do you need at Montserrat?
faqs.a: Three to four hours on the mountain, plus about an hour and a half of travel each way from Barcelona. Six to eight hours in all.
